claim: Individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) frequently exhibit cognitive and motor impairments and characteristics of autism.
source: Individuals with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) frequently exhibit cognitive and motor impairments and characteristics of autism.
evidence: This is a general statement about NF1 clinical features that is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: The cerebellum plays a critical role in motor control, cognition, and social interaction.
source: The cerebellum plays a critical role in motor control, cognition, and social interaction, suggesting that cerebellar defects likely contribute to NF1-associated neurodevelopmental disorders.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar function supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Nf1 inactivation during early, but not late stages of cerebellar development, disrupts neuronal lamination.
source: Here we show that Nf1 inactivation during early, but not late stages of cerebellar development, disrupts neuronal lamination, which is partially caused by overproduction of glia and subsequent disruption of the Bergmann glia (BG) scaffold.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from multiple mouse models shown in the figures.

claim: Disruption of neuronal lamination in Nf1-deficient cerebellum is partially caused by overproduction of glia and subsequent disruption of the Bergmann glia scaffold.
source: Here we show that Nf1 inactivation during early, but not late stages of cerebellar development, disrupts neuronal lamination, which is partially caused by overproduction of glia and subsequent disruption of the Bergmann glia (BG) scaffold.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased BG cells and disrupted scaffold in Nf1hGFAPCKO mice.

claim: Specific Nf1 inactivation in glutamatergic neuronal precursors causes premature differentiation of granule cell precursors.
source: Specific Nf1 inactivation in glutamatergic neuronal precursors causes premature differentiation of granule cell (GC) precursors and ectopic production of unipolar brush cells (UBCs), indirectly disrupting neuronal migration.
evidence: This is supported by BrdU pulse-chase experiments and MAP2 staining in Nf1Math1CKO mice shown in Figure 4.

claim: Specific Nf1 inactivation in glutamatergic neuronal precursors causes ectopic production of unipolar brush cells.
source: Specific Nf1 inactivation in glutamatergic neuronal precursors causes premature differentiation of granule cell (GC) precursors and ectopic production of unipolar brush cells (UBCs), indirectly disrupting neuronal migration.
evidence: This is supported by Tbr2 staining showing ectopic UBCs in the ML of Nf1Math1CKO mice in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Transient MEK inhibition during a neonatal window prevents cerebellar developmental defects in Nf1-deficient mice.
source: Transient MEK inhibition during a neonatal window prevents cerebellar developmental defects and improves long-term motor performance of Nf1-deficient mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing rescue of cerebellar defects in MEKi-treated mice in Figures 6, 7, and 8.

claim: Transient MEK inhibition during a neonatal window improves long-term motor performance of Nf1-deficient mice.
source: Transient MEK inhibition during a neonatal window prevents cerebellar developmental defects and improves long-term motor performance of Nf1-deficient mice.
evidence: This is supported by Rotarod test data showing improved motor performance in MEKi-treated mice in Figure 8.

claim: NF1 is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the NF1 tumor suppressor gene.
source: NF1 is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the NF1 tumor suppressor gene, which encodes neurofibromin, a negative regulator of proto-oncogene RAS (Cichowski and Jacks, 2001; Upadhyaya and Cooper, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NF1 genetics supported by citations.

claim: Neurofibromin is a negative regulator of proto-oncogene RAS.
source: NF1 is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the NF1 tumor suppressor gene, which encodes neurofibromin, a negative regulator of proto-oncogene RAS (Cichowski and Jacks, 2001; Upadhyaya and Cooper, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about neurofibromin function supported by citations.

claim: NF1 afflicts 1 in 2700 newborns.
source: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is a genetically inherited disorder that afflicts 1 in 2700 newborns (Evans et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an epidemiological fact supported by citation.

claim: RAS mediates multiple signaling pathways including ERK, PI3K and mTORC1.
source: RAS mediates multiple signaling pathways including extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) subfamily of mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK), phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) (Schubbert et al., 2007; Mendoza et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RAS signaling supported by citations.

claim: Approximately 50–80% of children with NF1 have impairments in fine and gross motor function.
source: Approximately 50–80% of children with NF1 have impairments in fine and gross motor function, which can be identified as early as at the toddler stage (Johnson et al., 2010; Krab et al., 2011; Lorenzo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by citations.

claim: Motor impairments in NF1 can be identified as early as at the toddler stage.
source: Approximately 50–80% of children with NF1 have impairments in fine and gross motor function, which can be identified as early as at the toddler stage (Johnson et al., 2010; Krab et al., 2011; Lorenzo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by citations.

claim: Impairments of gross motor skills and cognitive functioning in NF1 are often co-morbidities.
source: One recent study has shown that impairments of gross motor skills and cognitive functioning in NF1 are often co-morbidities, suggesting the potential existence of a common pathological mechanism underlying both motor and cognitive impairments (Champion et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by citation.

claim: About 80% of individuals with ASD exhibit anatomical abnormalities in the cerebellum.
source: About 80% of individuals with ASD exhibit anatomical abnormalities in the cerebellum, among which gliosis and Purkinje cell loss are most commonly identified (Bailey et al., 1998; Palmen et al., 2004; Vargas et al., 2005; Fatemi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by citations.

claim: Gliosis and Purkinje cell loss are the most commonly identified cerebellar abnormalities in individuals with ASD.
source: About 80% of individuals with ASD exhibit anatomical abnormalities in the cerebellum, among which gliosis and Purkinje cell loss are most commonly identified (Bailey et al., 1998; Palmen et al., 2004; Vargas et al., 2005; Fatemi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by citations.

claim: T2-weighted hyperintensities in the cerebellum are one of the most consistent brain abnormalities observed in individuals with NF1.
source: In addition, T2-weighted hyperintensities in the cerebellum are one of the most consistent brain abnormalities observed in individuals with NF1 (Feldmann et al., 2010; Payne et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by citations.

claim: Radial glial stem cells in the ventricular zone of the fourth ventricle give rise to all GABAergic neuronal lineages in the cerebellum.
source: Radial glial (RG) stem cells in the ventricular zone of the fourth ventricle (IV–VZ) give rise to all the GABAergic neuronal lineages—Purkinje cells and GABAergic interneurons including small deep cerebellar nuclei (DCN), Golgi, basket, and stellate cells (Sillitoe and Joyner, 2007; Buffo and Rossi, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar development supported by citations.

claim: Cerebellar astrocytes including Bergmann glia are derived from RG cells in the IV-VZ.
source: Cerebellar astrocytes including Bergmann glia (BG) are also derived from RG cells in the IV-VZ.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar development.

claim: The rhombic lip generates glutamatergic neuronal lineages including large DCN, unipolar brush cells, and granule cells.
source: A secondary germinal zone in the anterior portion of the rhombic lip (RL) generates glutamatergic neuronal lineages, including large DCN, unipolar brush cells (UBCs), and granule cells (GCs) (Englund et al., 2006; Sillitoe and Joyner, 2007; Mugnaini et al., 2011; Buffo and Rossi, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar development supported by citations.

claim: Purkinje cells and DCN are first generated between embryonic day 10.5–11.5 in mouse cerebellar neurogenesis.
source: At the onset of mouse cerebellar neurogenesis, projection neurons (Purkinje cells and DCN) are first generated between embryonic day 10.5–11.5 (E10.5–11.5) (Hatten, 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar development supported by citation.

claim: At E12.5, Math1-expressing proliferating precursors migrate out of the RL and spread across the surface of the cerebellum to form the external granule layer.
source: At E12.5, Math1 (also known as Atoh1)-expressing proliferating precursors migrate out of the RL and spread across the surface of the cerebellum to form the external granule layer (EGL) (Hatten, 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar development supported by citation.

claim: Around postnatal day 4–5, GC precursors in the EGL start to exit cell cycle and form a pre-migratory zone along the edge of the EGL.
source: Around postnatal day 4–5 (P4–5), GC precursors (GCPs) in the EGL start to exit cell cycle and form a pre-migratory zone along the edge of the EGL.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar development.

claim: Post-mitotic GCs migrate along the BG scaffold, across the molecular layer, and form the internal granule layer.
source: Post-mitotic cells then migrate along the BG scaffold, across the molecular layer (ML), and form the internal granule layer (IGL), where they become mature GCs and form synapses with Purkinje cells through mossy fibers (Hatten, 1999; Sillitoe and Joyner, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar development supported by citations.

claim: UBCs exit the RL at perinatal stages and migrate through the white matter into the IGL of the cerebellum.
source: UBCs exit the RL at perinatal stages and migrate through the white matter (WM) into the IGL of the cerebellum (Englund et al., 2005; Mugnaini et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about UBC development supported by citations.

claim: Nf1 heterozygous mice exhibit no defect in cerebellum-specific motor tests.
source: However, recent studies have shown that Nf1 heterozygous mice exhibit no defect in cerebellum-specific motor tests and that children with NF1 do not appear to have a general dysfunction of the cerebellum (Krab et al., 2011; van der Vaart et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Children with NF1 do not appear to have a general dysfunction of the cerebellum.
source: However, recent studies have shown that Nf1 heterozygous mice exhibit no defect in cerebellum-specific motor tests and that children with NF1 do not appear to have a general dysfunction of the cerebellum (Krab et al., 2011; van der Vaart et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Bi-allelic Nf1 inactivation in neural stem and progenitor cells during development is required for producing cellular pathologies in the cerebellum.
source: Thus, we hypothesize that bi-allelic Nf1 inactivation in neural stem and progenitor cells during development is required for producing cellular pathologies in the cerebellum.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors based on previous observations.

claim: hGFAP-cre targets RG stem cells in the IV-VZ around E12.5.
source: We first utilized a Cre transgenic strain controlled by human glial fibrillary acidic protein promoter (hGFAP-cre) to inactivate Nf1 in RG stem cells in the IV-VZ around E12.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,A′).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: RG cells targeted by hGFAP-cre in the E12.5 IV-VZ give rise to glutamatergic neuronal precursors populating the RL and astrocyte precursors producing astrocytes in cerebellar parenchyma.
source: RG cells targeted by hGFAP-cre in the E12.5 IV-VZ give rise to glutamatergic neuronal precursors populating the RL and astrocyte precursors producing astrocytes in cerebellar parenchyma (Zhu et al., 2005; Sillitoe and Joyner, 2007; Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about hGFAP-cre targeting supported by citations.

claim: The majority of oligodendrocytes in the cerebellum do not arise from RG cells in the IV-VZ, but from sources in the ventral-lateral mid/hindbrain.
source: Of note, the majority of oligodendrocytes in the cerebellum do not arise from RG cells in the IV-VZ, but from sources in the ventral-lateral mid/hindbrain (that was also targeted by hGFAP-cre) (Yang et al., 2008; Grimaldi et al., 2009; Mecklenburg et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about oligodendrocyte origins supported by citations.

claim: Glutamatergic neurons and glia, but not GABAergic Purkinje cells, were targeted by hGFAP-cre-mediated recombination.
source: Glutamatergic neurons (including GCs) and glia, but not GABAergic Purkinje cells, were targeted by hGFAP-cre-mediated recombination, revealed by β-galactosidase (β-gal) expression of the Rosa26-LacZ reporter and PCR analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B,B′) (Soriano, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nf1hGFAPCKO mice displayed severe defects in motor behaviors including abnormal hind limb crossing and vertical projection of tails.
source: The hGFAP-cre driven Nf1 conditional knockout mice (hereafter referred to as Nf1hGFAPCKO) displayed severe defects in motor behaviors including abnormal hind limb crossing and vertical projection of tails.
evidence: This is an observed phenotype in the Nf1hGFAPCKO mice.

claim: Most of the Nf1hGFAPCKO mice had ataxic hind limbs and some exhibited a unique 'handstand' behavior during postnatal stages.
source: Most of the Nf1hGFAPCKO mice had ataxic hind limbs and some exhibited a unique 'handstand' behavior during postnatal stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Video 1).
evidence: This is an observed phenotype in the Nf1hGFAPCKO mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Video 1.

claim: Neuronal lamination in all folia of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum was disrupted with a varying degree of severity.
source: As revealed by Hematoxylin & Eosin (H&E) staining, neuronal lamination in all folia of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum was disrupted with a varying degree of severity (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by H&E staining data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The patterning of Calbindin+ Purkinje cells was disrupted in severely affected areas of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
source: In the severely affected areas (e.g., folia V/VI), the patterning of Calbindin+ Purkinje cells was disrupted, and failed to form the single Purkinje cell layer (PCL) observed in controls (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Calbindin staining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The disorganized Purkinje cells in Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum still expressed neurofibromin.
source: Since hGFAP-cre was not targeted to Purkinje cells, the disorganized Purkinje cells still expressed neurofibromin (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) (Zhu et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by neurofibromin staining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The disrupted patterning of Purkinje cells in Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum is non-cell-autonomous.
source: Thus, the disrupted patterning of Purkinje cells must be non-cell-autonomous, and secondary to Nf1 inactivation in other cerebellar neurons and/or glia.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Purkinje cells still express neurofibromin but are disorganized.

claim: No overt defect was identified in the Nf1L7CKO cerebellum where Nf1 was specifically inactivated in Purkinje cells.
source: No overt defect was identified in the Nf1L7CKO cerebellum, confirming that Nf1 is relatively dispensable in the development of Purkinje cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Nf1 is relatively dispensable in the development of Purkinje cells.
source: No overt defect was identified in the Nf1L7CKO cerebellum, confirming that Nf1 is relatively dispensable in the development of Purkinje cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by the lack of defects in Nf1L7CKO cerebellum shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: The boundary between ML, PCL and IGL in the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum was less clearly defined compared to normal cerebellum.
source: In contrast to the normal cerebellum with three distinct laminar layers—ML, PCL and IGL, the boundary between these three layers in the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum was less clearly defined, and the cell number in the ML was dramatically increased with a concomitant reduction of cells in the IGL (Figure 1A–A′′; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A′).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The cell number in the ML was dramatically increased with a concomitant reduction of cells in the IGL in the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
source: In contrast to the normal cerebellum with three distinct laminar layers—ML, PCL and IGL, the boundary between these three layers in the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum was less clearly defined, and the cell number in the ML was dramatically increased with a concomitant reduction of cells in the IGL (Figure 1A–A′′; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1A′ and A′′.

claim: Some abnormally accumulated cells in the Nf1hGFAPCKO ML were found on the pial surface of the cerebellum, corresponding to the EGL.
source: Some of the abnormally accumulated cells in the Nf1hGFAPCKO ML were found on the pial surface of the cerebellum, corresponding to the EGL—a structure that transiently exists during development, but disappears after the completion of GC migration (arrows, Figure 1Ab′′).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: No significant difference was found in the total number of NeuN+ neurons in the ML and IGL between the control and Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
source: No significant difference was found in the total number of NeuN+ neurons in the ML and IGL (per surface area) between the control and Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1D′.

claim: The distribution of NeuN+ neurons was greatly altered between the control and Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellar cortex.
source: Instead, the distribution of NeuN+ neurons was greatly altered between the control and Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellar cortex—the number of NeuN+ neurons was increased over 20-fold in the mutant ML (Figure 1D,D′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1D′.

claim: The number of NeuN+ neurons was increased over 20-fold in the Nf1hGFAPCKO ML.
source: Instead, the distribution of NeuN+ neurons was greatly altered between the control and Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellar cortex—the number of NeuN+ neurons was increased over 20-fold in the mutant ML (Figure 1D,D′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1D′.

claim: 60% of abnormally accumulated neurons in the Nf1hGFAPCKO ML were positive for GABARα6.
source: While no cells in the control ML expressed GABA receptor alpha 6 subunit (GABARα6), a marker for mature GCs, 60% of abnormally accumulated neurons in the Nf1hGFAPCKO ML were positive for GABARα6 (Figure 1D,D′′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1D′′.

claim: A subset of Nf1-deficient GCs fail to migrate inward from the EGL, across ML and PCL, to the IGL.
source: These observations are most consistent with a model wherein a subset of Nf1-deficient GCs fail to migrate inward from the EGL, across ML and PCL, to the IGL.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of increased neurons in the ML and reduced neurons in the IGL.

claim: In the control cerebellum, BG cells were located either immediately below or interspersed between Purkinje cell bodies, forming a Purkinje cell and BG monolayer.
source: In the control cerebellum, BG cells were located either immediately below or interspersed between Purkinje cell bodies, forming a Purkinje cell and BG (PC/BG) monolayer (arrows, Figure 1E,F) (Buffo and Rossi, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by BLBP staining data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Nf1-deficient BG cells failed to form a PC/BG monolayer due to excess number and mispositioning of BG cells.
source: In contrast, Nf1-deficient BG cells failed to form a PC/BG monolayer, which appeared to be caused by excess number and mispositioning of BG cells (arrows, Figure 1E,E′,F).
evidence: This is supported by BLBP staining and quantification data shown in Figure 1E,E′,F.

claim: A strong correlation was observed between the severity of neuronal patterning defects and the abnormalities in the number and position of BG cells and the integrity of the PC/BG monolayer.
source: A strong correlation was observed between the severity of neuronal patterning defects and the abnormalities in the number and position of BG cells and the integrity of the PC/BG monolayer (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The capacity of Nf1-deficient BG cells to extend their processes to the pial surface was relatively uncompromised.
source: Importantly, the capacity of Nf1-deficient BG cells to extend their processes to the pial surface was relatively uncompromised—this was even true for some of the BG cells that were located in the areas outside the PC/BG layer in the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by GFAP staining data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Inactivation of Nf1 during early embryonic stages overproduces BG cells, impairing the formation of the PC/BG monolayer and the alignment of the BG scaffold.
source: Based on these results, we propose a model wherein inactivation of Nf1 during early embryonic stages overproduces BG cells, thus impairing the formation of the PC/BG monolayer, and consequently, the alignment of the BG scaffold.
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their experimental observations.

claim: The defective BG scaffold non-cell-autonomously arrests GC migration and subsequently disrupts Purkinje cell patterning during cerebellar development.
source: The defective BG scaffold non-cell-autonomously arrests GC migration and subsequently disrupts Purkinje cell patterning during cerebellar development.
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their experimental observations.

claim: No defect was observed in the overall structure and the distribution of RL-derived Math1+ neuronal precursors in the EGL, Purkinje cells or BLBP+ cells in the E17.5 Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
source: No defect was observed in the overall structure and the distribution of RL-derived Math1+ neuronal precursors in the EGL, Purkinje cells or BLBP+ cells in the E17.5 Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No difference was identified in the number of BLBP+ RG cells in the IV-VZ of E17.5 Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
source: Furthermore, no difference was identified in the number of BLBP+ RG cells (including proliferating BLBP+Ki67+ population) in the IV-VZ (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: An increased number of both total BLBP+ and proliferating BLBP+Ki67+ cells was observed in the PWM of the E17.5 Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
source: However, an increased number of both total BLBP+ and proliferating BLBP+Ki67+ cells was observed in the prospective white matter (PWM) of the E17.5 Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum compared to controls (Figure 2A,A′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2A′.

claim: Mitotic index was significantly increased in the E17.5 Nf1hGFAPCKO PWM.
source: More importantly, mitotic index, determined by the ratio of proliferating BLBP+Ki67+ cells to the total BLBP+ cells, was significantly increased in the E17.5 Nf1hGFAPCKO PWM (Figure 2A,A′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2A′.

claim: Nf1 specifically constrains the proliferation of astrocyte precursors in the PWM, but not multipotent RG cells of the IV-VZ in the E17.5 cerebellum.
source: These observations suggest that Nf1 specifically constrains the proliferation of astrocyte precursors in the PWM, but not multipotent RG cells of the IV-VZ in the E17.5 cerebellum.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential proliferation patterns observed in PWM vs IV-VZ.

claim: The increased mitotic index was no longer detected in the more differentiated BLBP+ BG cells in the anterior folia at P0.5, but only in the posterior folia (IX and X).
source: Unexpectedly, the increased mitotic index was no longer detected in the more differentiated BLBP+ BG cells in the anterior folia, but only in the posterior folia (IX and X) of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum where BG cells had not formed a rudimentary PC/BG layer at P0.5 (Figure 2B,B′,2C,C′; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2B′ and 2C′.

claim: An increase of cells with strong nuclear BLBP staining in the P0.5 Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum was identified, suggesting a persistent increase of proliferating BG cells into postnatal stages.
source: Consistently, an increase of cells with strong nuclear BLBP staining in the P0.5 Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum was identified, suggesting a persistent increase of proliferating BG cells into postnatal stages (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by BLBP staining data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: BLBP+ cells in the PWM still exhibited an increased mitotic index in the P0.5 Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
source: Similarly, BLBP+ cells in the PWM, the precursors of WM astrocytes, still exhibited an increased mitotic index in the P0.5 Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–D′′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D′′.

claim: At P8, the mitotic index of BLBP+ BG cells was no longer increased in the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum, despite a significant increase of both total BLBP+ and proliferating BLBP+Ki67+ BG cells.
source: At P8 when BG cells had formed a rudimentary PC/BG layer throughout the cerebellum, the mitotic index of BLBP+ BG cells was no longer increased in the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum, despite a significant increase of both total BLBP+ and proliferating BLBP+Ki67+ BG cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,E′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E′.

claim: Nf1 constrains the proliferation of the BG/astrocyte lineage cells specifically at an intermediate precursor stage located in the PWM, but not at an earlier RG stem cell stage or a more differentiated BG stage.
source: Together, these results suggest that Nf1 constrains the proliferation of the BG/astrocyte lineage cells specifically at an intermediate precursor stage located in the PWM, but not at an earlier RG stem cell stage or a more differentiated BG stage, thereby identifying a window of susceptibility of astrocyte precursors to Nf1 mutation.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal and spatial patterns of proliferation defects observed.

claim: Excess BG cells failed to form a similar PC/BG layer at P8, but were aberrantly distributed throughout the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellar cortex.
source: At P8, control BG cells labeled by nuclear Cre staining formed a rudimentary 2 to 3 cell-layer lining within the APC+ Purkinje cell layer (Figure 2E). In contrast, excess BG cells failed to form a similar PC/BG layer, but were aberrantly distributed throughout the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellar cortex (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is supported by Cre and APC staining data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Some Nf1-deficient BG cells extended their processes from ectopic locations of the cerebellum including the WM, ML and IGL, accompanied by misalignment of the BG scaffold.
source: Consequently, some Nf1-deficient BG cells extended their processes from ectopic locations of the cerebellum including the WM, ML and IGL, accompanied by misalignment of the BG scaffold (Figure 2E,F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by GFAP staining data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: All major defects observed in BG cells, GCs and Purkinje cells of the adult Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum were identified at P8.
source: Indeed, all major defects observed in BG cells, GCs and Purkinje cells of the adult Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum were identified at P8, suggesting that these defects manifest during neonatal stages (Figure 2G–H′; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–H′′).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of P8 and adult cerebella.

claim: Overproduction of astrocyte precursors during embryonic stages is the primary defect causing both glial and neuronal abnormalities in the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
source: These results supports a model wherein overproduction of astrocyte precursors during embryonic stages is the primary defect causing both glial and neuronal abnormalities in the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their experimental observations.

claim: NCreER-targeted cells analyzed at P21 were restricted to glial lineage cells in both the control and Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum with only one exception in folium X.
source: Upon a single TM pulse at E17.5, NCreER-targeted cells analyzed at P21 were restricted to glial lineage cells in both the control and Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum with only one exception in folium X, where a significant number of both glia and GCs in the IGL were targeted (Figure 3A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by β-gal staining data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: No alteration in the number of BLBP+ cells or the BG scaffold was observed in any of the anterior folia (I to V) between the control and Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum.
source: No alteration in the number of BLBP+ cells or the BG scaffold was observed in any of the anterior folia (I to V) between the control and Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by BLBP staining data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Neurons did not abnormally accumulate in the ML of the anterior Nf1NCreERCKO folia.
source: Furthermore, neurons did not abnormally accumulate in the ML of the anterior Nf1NCreERCKO folia (Figure 3A,A′; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,D′).
evidence: This is supported by NeuN staining and quantification data shown in Figure 3A′.

claim: In folium X, the number of Nf1-deficient BLBP+ cells (BLBP+β-gal+) was significantly increased in the Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum.
source: In folium X, the number of Nf1-deficient BLBP+ cells (BLBP+β-gal+) was significantly increased, though this was subtle compared to the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The other posterior folia (e.g., VI–IX) exhibited a slightly, but significantly increased number of Nf1-deficient BLBP+ cells in the Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum.
source: Indeed, the other posterior folia (e.g., VI–IX) exhibited a slightly, but significantly increased number of Nf1-deficient BLBP+ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,C′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C′.

claim: The overproduction of BLBP+β-gal+ BG cells in the posterior folia of the Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum appeared to be caused by cell-autonomous Nf1 inactivation.
source: The overproduction of BLBP+β-gal+ BG cells in the posterior folia of the Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum appeared to be caused by cell-autonomous Nf1 inactivation, as the number of non-NCreER-targeted BLBP+β-gal- cells in the same areas was not altered (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only β-gal+ cells were increased.

claim: The overproduction of BLBP+ BG cells was accompanied by focal misalignment of the BG scaffold and abnormal accumulation of both Nf1-deficient and Nf1-intact neurons in the ML of the Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum.
source: Importantly, the overproduction of BLBP+ BG cells was accompanied by focal misalignment of the BG scaffold and abnormal accumulation of both Nf1-deficient (NeuN+β-gal+) and Nf1-intact (NeuN+β-gal−) neurons in the ML of the Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum (Figure 3B,D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by NeuN and β-gal staining data shown in Figure 3B,D.

claim: Overproduction of astrocytic lineage causes impaired formation of the PC/BG monolayer and BG scaffold, non-cell-autonomously arresting GC migration.
source: These results suggest that overproduction of this particular astrocytic lineage causes impaired formation of the PC/BG monolayer and BG scaffold, non-cell-autonomously arresting GC migration.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both Nf1-deficient and Nf1-intact neurons accumulate in the ML.

claim: Math1-cre-mediated recombination was almost exclusively restricted to the cells in the IGL of the adult cerebellum.
source: Math1-cre-mediated recombination was almost exclusively restricted to the cells in the IGL of the adult cerebellum (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by X-gal staining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: β-gal+ cells were restricted to GCs in the IGL, but not Purkinje cells or glial cells, including BG cells in the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum.
source: Double staining of β-gal and other lineage markers showed that β-gal+ cells were restricted to GCs in the IGL, but not Purkinje cells or glial cells, including BG cells (Figure 4B,B′).
evidence: This is supported by double staining data shown in Figure 4B,B′.

claim: No defect in Purkinje cells or glial cells, particularly the BG scaffold, was observed in the adult Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum.
source: No defect in Purkinje cells or glial cells, particularly the BG scaffold, was observed in the adult Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum (Figure 4B,B′).
evidence: This is supported by staining data shown in Figure 4B,B′.

claim: The Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum exhibited abnormal accumulation of cells in the ML including some on the pial surface.
source: However, the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum did exhibit one major defect observed in the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum—abnormal accumulation of cells in the ML including some on the pial surface (arrows, Figure 4A,B–B′′; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,A′).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The increased neuronal density in the ML of the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum was caused by abnormal accumulation of Nf1-deficient NeuN+ neurons in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: The number of NeuN+β-gal+, but not NeuN+β-gal− neurons, was significantly increased, suggesting that the increased neuronal density in the ML of the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum was caused by abnormal accumulation of Nf1-deficient NeuN+ neurons in a cell-autonomous manner (Figure 4A,B,B′′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4B′′.

claim: Abnormal accumulation of neurons was evident in the ML of the P8 Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum, suggesting a developmental defect during neonatal stages.
source: Despite that no defect in the BG scaffold was observed, abnormal accumulation of neurons was evident in the ML of the P8 Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum, suggesting a developmental defect during neonatal stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 24 hr after BrdU pulse, BrdU+ cells in both the control and Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum remained exclusively in the EGL and exhibited similar cell cycle profiles.
source: 24 hr after pulse, BrdU+ cells in both the control and Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum remained exclusively in the EGL and exhibited similar cell cycle profiles, suggesting that Nf1 is not required for proliferation and cell-cycle exit of GC precursors (GCPs) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–C′′).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU and Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Nf1 is not required for proliferation and cell-cycle exit of GC precursors.
source: 24 hr after pulse, BrdU+ cells in both the control and Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum remained exclusively in the EGL and exhibited similar cell cycle profiles, suggesting that Nf1 is not required for proliferation and cell-cycle exit of GC precursors (GCPs) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–C′′).
evidence: This is inferred from the similar cell cycle profiles observed.

claim: 32 hr after BrdU pulse, many BrdU+ cells in the Nf1Math1CKO ML already acquired MAP2 expression with rounded nuclei—typical neuronal differentiation features for mature GCs in the IGL.
source: However, 32 hr after BrdU pulse, a subset of BrdU+ cells in the control cerebellum started departing from the EGL and entered the ML, not yet reaching the IGL (Figure 4C). While migrating GCs in the control ML did not express MAP2, a marker for mature GCs in the IGL, and had nuclei with a spindle-shaped migrating morphology, many BrdU+ cells in the Nf1Math1CKO ML already acquired MAP2 expression with rounded nuclei—typical neuronal differentiation features for mature GCs in the IGL (arrows, Figure 4C,C′).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU and MAP2 staining data shown in Figure 4C,C′.

claim: After 48-hr BrdU pulse, BrdU+MAP2+ cells in the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum progressively accumulated in the ML and EGL whereas control BrdU+ cells did not express MAP2 until they reached the IGL.
source: After 48-hr BrdU pulse, BrdU+MAP2+ cells in the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum progressively accumulated in the ML and EGL whereas control BrdU+ cells did not express MAP2 until they reached the IGL (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,D′).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU and MAP2 staining data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Newly generated neurons were abnormally accumulated in the ML/EGL of the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum, leading to an increased number of differentiated BrdU+Ki67− and p27+ cells in the ML/EGL with a concomitant reduction in the IGL.
source: Newly generated neurons were abnormally accumulated in the ML/EGL of the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum, leading to an increased number of differentiated BrdU+Ki67− and p27+ cells in the ML/EGL with a concomitant reduction in the IGL (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,E′,F,F′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E′,F′.

claim: A subset of Nf1-deficient GCPs undergo accelerated and premature neuronal differentiation, thereby arresting their migration in the EGL and ML.
source: These observations suggest that a subset of Nf1-deficient GCPs undergo accelerated and premature neuronal differentiation, thereby arresting their migration in the EGL and ML.
evidence: This is inferred from the BrdU pulse-chase experiments showing premature MAP2 expression.

claim: 2 days after being plated in culture, significantly more Nf1-deficient GCPs expressed MAP2 than control cells, confirming an accelerated neuronal differentiation rate in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: This conclusion was further supported by in vitro studies. 2 days after being plated in culture, significantly more Nf1-deficient GCPs expressed MAP2 than control cells, confirming an accelerated neuronal differentiation rate in a cell-autonomous manner (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G,G′).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro differentiation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G,G′.

claim: Nf1-deficient GCs could efficiently interact with wild-type glia in a co-culture system and migrated normally in a trans-well migration assay.
source: Importantly, Nf1-deficient GCs could efficiently interact with wild-type glia in a co-culture system and migrated normally in a trans-well migration assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H,H′).
evidence: This is supported by co-culture and trans-well migration assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H,H′.

claim: Nf1 is indirectly required for GC migration by suppressing GCPs to undergo premature terminal differentiation and ectopic differentiation to Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs in the EGL and ML.
source: Thus, our study demonstrates that Nf1 is indirectly required for GC migration by suppressing GCPs to undergo premature terminal differentiation and ectopic differentiation to Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs in the EGL and ML.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from both in vivo and in vitro experimental data.

claim: Many of the prematurely differentiated neurons in the ML of the P8 Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum expressed Tbr2, a marker specific for UBCs in the cerebellum.
source: Strikingly, many of the prematurely differentiated neurons in the ML of the P8 Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum expressed Tbr2, a marker specific for UBCs in the cerebellum (Figure 4E,E′).
evidence: This is supported by Tbr2 staining data shown in Figure 4E,E′.

claim: Tbr2+ cells including the newly generated Tbr2+BrdU+ cells were readily identified in the P8 Nf1Math1CKO EGL and ML.
source: While Tbr2+ UBCs were rarely identified in the control ML (Englund et al., 2006), Tbr2+ cells including the newly generated Tbr2+BrdU+ cells were readily identified in the P8 Nf1Math1CKO EGL and ML (Figure 4E,E′,F,F′).
evidence: This is supported by Tbr2 and BrdU staining data shown in Figure 4E,E′,F,F′.

claim: Tbr2 expression was ectopically acquired in a subset of newly generated cells even before migrating out of the EGL.
source: Tbr2 expression was ectopically acquired in a subset of newly generated cells even before migrating out of the EGL, and over time these Tbr2+BrdU+ double-positive cells progressively accumulated from the EGL, ML to IGL (Figure 4F,F′,G,G′).
evidence: This is supported by Tbr2 and BrdU staining data shown in Figure 4F,F′,G,G′.

claim: Nf1 inactivation ectopically generates Tbr2+ UBCs from GCPs in the EGL, which appear to migrate along the same pathway as GCs.
source: These observations demonstrate that Nf1 inactivation ectopically generates Tbr2+ UBCs from GCPs in the EGL, which appear to migrate along the same pathway as GCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of Tbr2+ cells in the EGL and their progressive accumulation in ML and IGL.

claim: Cells with the classic morphology of UBCs were identified in the ML of the P8 Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum, but not in the control cerebellum.
source: More importantly, cells with the classic morphology of UBCs were identified in the ML of the P8 Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum, but not in the control cerebellum, indicating that these Tbr2+ cells not only acquire UBC-specific Tbr2 expression, but also undergo morphological differentiation of UBCs (Figure 4H) (Mugnaini and Floris, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by Golgi staining data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Approximately 30–40% of abnormally accumulated NeuN+ neurons in the ML of the adult Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum expressed Tbr2.
source: Consequently, approximately 30–40% of abnormally accumulated NeuN+ neurons in the ML of the adult Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum expressed Tbr2 (Figure 4I,I′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4I′.

claim: Nf1 plays cell-autonomous functions in suppressing GCPs to ectopically differentiate into UBCs.
source: Together, these observations identify cell-autonomous Nf1 functions in suppressing GCPs to ectopically differentiate into UBCs (Figure 4J,J′).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing ectopic UBC generation in Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum.

claim: A dramatic increase of Tbr2+ cells was observed in the ML throughout the adult Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum, which was most evident in folia V/VI.
source: Indeed, a dramatic increase of Tbr2+ cells was also observed in the ML throughout the adult Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum, which was most evident in folia V/VI (Figure 5A–A′′).
evidence: This is supported by Tbr2 staining and quantification data shown in Figure 5A–A′′.

claim: The increase of Tbr2+ cells in the ML (98%) and IGL (94%) of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum was almost entirely contributed by UBCs that expressed a moderate level of Tbr2 as well as NeuN (Tbr2+NeuN+).
source: The increase of Tbr2+ cells in the ML (98%) and IGL (94%) of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum was almost entirely contributed by UBCs that expressed a moderate level of Tbr2 as well as NeuN (Tbr2+NeuN+) (arrows, Figure 5B,B′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5B′.

claim: Almost all UBCs in the control folium V expressed high levels of Tbr2, but no NeuN (Tbr2highNeuN−) and were mainly distributed in the IGL.
source: Almost all UBCs in the control folium V expressed high levels of Tbr2, but no NeuN (Tbr2highNeuN−) and were mainly distributed in the IGL (arrowheads, Figure 5B,B′).
evidence: This is supported by Tbr2 and NeuN staining data shown in Figure 5B,B′.

claim: The number of Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs was not significantly different between the control and the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
source: It should be noted that the number of Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs was not significantly different between the control and the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the quantification data.

claim: Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs in the ML and IGL of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum expressed CRhigh at a significantly lower percentage (36% and 38%) than Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs (67%) typically observed in the IGL.
source: CRhigh is a marker for a subset of UBCs due to its low expression in granule cells (Mugnaini et al., 2011). Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs in the ML and IGL of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum expressed CRhigh at a significantly lower percentage (36% and 38%) than Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs (67%) typically observed in the IGL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,A′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A′.

claim: The absolute number of Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs was similar in the ML of folium V between the Nf1Math1CKO and Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
source: Importantly, the absolute number of Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs was similar in the ML of folium V between the Nf1Math1CKO and Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum, further supporting the notion that ectopic generation of these UBCs results from loss of cell-autonomous Nf1 function in the glutamatergic neuronal lineages (Figure 4I′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4I′.

claim: Ectopic Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs were continuously generated in the ML and IGL of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum during postnatal stages.
source: Similar to the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum, ectopic Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs were continuously generated in the ML and IGL of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum during postnatal stages (arrows, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,B′,C,C′), well beyond the developmental window of the generation of control Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs (Figure 4J,J′).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU pulse-chase data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,B′,C,C′.

claim: The Tbr2+ UBCs ectopically generated in both the Nf1Math1CKO and Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum are different from those previously described in the normal cerebellum in 6 critical aspects.
source: Together, these observations demonstrate that the Tbr2+ UBCs ectopically generated in both the Nf1Math1CKO and Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum are different from those previously described in the normal cerebellum in 6 critical aspects: (1) the marker expression, Tbr2+NeuN+ vs Tbr2highNeuN−, (2) the low vs high percentage expressing CRhigh, (3) the location, ML and IGL vs IGL, (4) the developmental origin, precursors in the EGL vs RL, (5) the timing of birth, neonatal vs embryonic stages, and (6) the migratory pathway, EGL-ML-IGL vs RL-PWM-IGL.
evidence: This is a summary of the differences observed between the two UBC sublineages.

claim: Two UBC sublineages exist in the cerebellum.
source: Thus, we suggest the existence of two UBC sublineages.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observed differences between Tbr2+NeuN+ and Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs.

claim: The majority of GABARα6-negative neurons were Tbr2+NeuN+ cells in the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
source: Importantly, the majority of GABARα6-negative neurons were Tbr2+NeuN+ cells, while no significant difference was observed in GABAergic neurons between the control and Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E,E′).
evidence: This is supported by staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E,E′.

claim: Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs are the major contributors to the non-GCs abnormally accumulated in the ML of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
source: These observations suggest that Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs are the major contributors to the non-GCs abnormally accumulated in the ML of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum (Figure 1D–D′′).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most GABARα6-negative neurons are Tbr2+NeuN+ cells.

claim: The number of Tbr2+ cells was significantly increased in the ML of the folium X of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
source: As observed in the rest of mutant folia, the number of Tbr2+ cells was also significantly increased in the ML of the folium X of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum (Figure 5C,C′; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5C′.

claim: The number of Tbr2+ cells was unexpectedly reduced in the IGL of folium X of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum concomitant with ectopic presence of Tbr2+ cells in the surrounding WM.
source: However, the number of Tbr2+ cells was unexpectedly reduced in the IGL of folium X of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum concomitant with ectopic presence of Tbr2+ cells in the surrounding WM (Figure 5C,C′; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5C′.

claim: The Tbr2+NeuN+ UBC sublineage contributed to almost the entire UBC population in the ML of both the control (97%) and Nf1hGFAPCKO (99%) folium X.
source: As in Folium V, the Tbr2+NeuN+ UBC sublineage contributed to almost the entire UBC population in the ML of both the control (97%) and Nf1hGFAPCKO (99%) folium X (Figure 5D,D′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5D′.

claim: Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs were indeed increased in the IGL of Nf1hGFAPCKO folium X, and thus the reduction of Tbr2+ UBCs was exclusively attributed to a decreased number of Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs in the IGL.
source: Similarly, Tbr2+NeuN+ UBCs were indeed increased in the IGL of Nf1hGFAPCKO folium X, and thus the reduction of Tbr2+ UBCs was exclusively attributed to a decreased number of Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs in the IGL (Figure 5D,D′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5D′.

claim: UBCs in both the Nf1hGFAPCKO WM and IGL were the Tbr2highNeuN− sublineage, which was normally located in the IGL of the control cerebellum with a higher percentage expressing CRhigh.
source: Consistently, UBCs in both the Nf1hGFAPCKO WM and IGL were the Tbr2highNeuN− sublineage, which was normally located in the IGL of the control cerebellum with a higher percentage expressing CRhigh (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–B′′).
evidence: This is supported by staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–B′′.

claim: The total number of Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs was almost identical when the number in the WM and IGL of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum was combined to compare with the number in the IGL of the control cerebellum, suggesting arrested migration in the WM.
source: More importantly, the total number of Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs was almost identical, when the number of the Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs in the WM and IGL of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum was combined to compare with the number of Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs in the IGL of the control cerebellum, suggesting arrested migration in the WM (Figure 5D–D′′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5D–D′′.

claim: No alteration in the number and distribution of Tbr2+ UBCs was observed at early stages of UBC development before they migrated out of the RL or entered the PWM during perinatal stages.
source: Consistently, no alteration in the number and distribution of Tbr2+ UBCs was observed at early stages of UBC development before they migrated out of the RL or entered the PWM during perinatal stages (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,C′).
evidence: This is supported by Tbr2 staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,C′.

claim: Abnormal accumulation of Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs in the Nf1hGFAPCKO WM was evident at P8, a time point when normal UBCs had already migrated through the PWM and entered the IGL.
source: Instead, abnormal accumulation of Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs in the Nf1hGFAPCKO WM was evident at P8, a time point when normal UBCs had already migrated through the PWM and entered the IGL (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D,D′).
evidence: This is supported by Tbr2 staining and quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D,D′.

claim: The abnormal accumulation of Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs in the WM of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum was caused by arrested migration of UBCs in the PWM on the way from the RL to the IGL during neonatal development.
source: Together, these results suggest that the abnormal accumulation of Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs in the WM of the Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum was caused by arrested migration of UBCs in the PWM on the way from the RL to the IGL during neonatal development (Englund et al., 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal and spatial patterns of UBC accumulation in the WM.

claim: No ectopic Tbr2+ UBCs were observed in the WM of the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum, suggesting a non-cell-autonomous mechanism.
source: Importantly, no ectopic Tbr2+ UBCs were observed in the WM of the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum, suggesting a non-cell-autonomous mechanism (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by Tbr2 staining data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Abnormally increased numbers of GFAP+BLBP− astrocytes were observed in the enlarged WM of the adult Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum.
source: Consistently, abnormally increased numbers of GFAP+BLBP− astrocytes were observed in the enlarged WM of the adult Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebellum, raising the possibility that excess astrocytes in the WM could impede the migration of UBCs from the WM to the IGL (Figure 5E,E′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5E′.

claim: A subpopulation of Tbr2high UBCs, all of which were wild-type for Nf1, ectopically accumulated in the WM of folium X in the TM-induced Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum.
source: In the TM-induced Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum where the number of glial cells was increased specifically in the posterior folia, a subpopulation of Tbr2high UBCs, all of which were wild-type for Nf1 (not labeled by β-gal expression), ectopically accumulated in the WM of folium X (arrowheads, Figure 5G,G′).
evidence: This is supported by Tbr2 and β-gal staining data shown in Figure 5G,G′.

claim: Excess Tbr2+ UBCs in the ML of the TM-induced Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum appears to result from overproduction of Nf1-deficient Tbr2+β-gal+ UBCs—a cell-autonomous mechanism.
source: Of note, excess Tbr2+ UBCs in the ML of the TM-induced Nf1NCreERCKO cerebellum appears to result from overproduction of Nf1-deficient Tbr2+β-gal+ UBCs—a cell-autonomous mechanism as described in the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum (Figure 5G,G′′).
evidence: This is supported by Tbr2 and β-gal staining data shown in Figure 5G,G′′.

claim: Overproduction of astrocytes in the WM of the Nf1hGFAPCKO and Nf1NCreERCKO cerebella produces a physical barrier that exerts non-cell-autonomous effect, arresting migration of Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs in the WM.
source: These results suggest that overproduction of astrocytes in the WM of the Nf1hGFAPCKO and Nf1NCreERCKO cerebella produces a physical barrier that exerts non-cell-autonomous effect, arresting migration of Tbr2highNeuN− UBCs in the WM.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Nf1-intact UBCs accumulate in the WM where excess astrocytes are present.

claim: Erk/MAPK was the only downstream signaling pathway that was consistently hyperactivated in Nf1Math1CKO cerebella.
source: Although Western blot analysis showed a significant reduction of neurofibromin expression, Erk/MAPK was the only downstream signaling pathway that was consistently hyperactivated in Nf1Math1CKO cerebella (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Cell cultures with enriched P6 GCPs showed almost a complete loss of neurofibromin expression with a robust increase of Erk activation.
source: Consistent with the specificity of Math1-cre transgene, cell cultures with enriched P6 GCPs showed almost a complete loss of neurofibromin expression with a robust increase of Erk activation (Figure 6A′).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A′.

claim: A high level of phosphorylated Erk expression was observed in a subset of IGL cells, while a low level in the ML and a complete absence of p-Erk in the EGL was found in the control cerebellum at P8.
source: A high level of phosphorylated Erk (p-Erk) expression was observed in a subset of IGL cells, while a low level in the ML and a complete absence of p-Erk in the EGL was found in the control cerebellum at P8 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by p-Erk staining data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A robust increase of p-Erk expression was observed in the P8 Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum including the inner edge of the EGL, the ML, and IGL.
source: A robust increase of p-Erk expression was observed in the P8 Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum including the inner edge of the EGL (pre-migratory zone), the ML, and IGL (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by p-Erk staining data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The NeuN+ neurons abnormally accumulated in the ML of the P8 Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum expressed a high level of p-Erk.
source: Importantly, the NeuN+ neurons abnormally accumulated in the ML of the P8 Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum expressed a high level of p-Erk (arrows, Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by p-Erk and NeuN staining data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Nf1 is a major regulator that suppresses Erk signaling in migrating GCs in the pre-migratory EGL and migratory zone (ML) of the developing cerebellum.
source: These results demonstrate that Nf1 is a major regulator that suppresses Erk signaling in migrating GCs in the pre-migratory EGL and migratory zone (ML) of the developing cerebellum.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased p-Erk expression in Nf1-deficient cells in the EGL and ML.

claim: MEK inhibition completely eliminated ectopic Tbr2 expression in the ML of MEKi-treated Nf1Math1CKO cerebella.
source: Strikingly, MEK inhibition completely eliminated ectopic Tbr2 expression in the ML of MEKi-treated Nf1Math1CKO cerebella (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by Tbr2 staining data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: MEK inhibition consistently reduced over 60% of abnormally accumulated neurons in the ML of the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum.
source: MEK inhibition consistently reduced over 60% of abnormally accumulated neurons in the ML of the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum (Figure 6C,C′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6C′.

claim: Rapamycin treatment had no benefit on neuronal defects in the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum, but caused adverse effects on neuronal migration in both the control and mutant cerebellum.
source: Rapamycin treatment had no benefit on neuronal defects in the Nf1Math1CKO cerebellum, but caused adverse effects on neuronal migration in both the control and mutant cerebellum (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nf1-mediated MEK/Erk inhibition is the major mechanism underlying the suppression of a subset of GCPs that otherwise would undergo premature differentiation and ectopically adopt a UBC fate in the developing cerebellum.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that Nf1-mediated MEK/Erk inhibition is the major mechanism underlying the suppression of a subset of GCPs that otherwise would undergo premature differentiation and ectopically adopt a UBC fate in the developing cerebellum.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MEKi treatment experiments showing rescue of neuronal defects.

claim: 9 out of 14 MEKi-treated Nf1hGFAPCKO mice (G-responders) exhibited a significant rescue in the number of neurons abnormally accumulated in the ML of the developing cerebellum.
source: Of 14 MEKi-treated Nf1hGFAPCKO cerebella analyzed, 9 mice (good-responders or G-responders) exhibited a significant rescue in the number of neurons abnormally accumulated in the ML of the developing cerebellum at a level similar to what was achieved in the MEKi-treated Nf1Math1CKO mice (green color, Figure 7A–A′′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7A–A′′.

claim: 5 of the MEKi-treated Nf1hGFAPCKO mice (P-responders) only exhibited marginal improvement in the neuronal defect.
source: However, the remaining 5 of the MEKi-treated Nf1hGFAPCKO mice (poor-responders or P-responders) only exhibited marginal improvement in the neuronal defect (yellow color, Figure 7A–A′′).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7A–A′′.

claim: G- and P-responders could be readily distinguished by the presence or absence of rescues in the number of BG cells, alignment of the BG scaffold, the number of mispositioned Purkinje cells and arrested UBCs in the WM.
